rows: Types and components of computer systems

Hardware is the physical components of a computer system.
Internal hardware is inside the computer, such as the motherboard, RAM and ROM.
External hardware includes peripherals connected to the computer, such as a keyboard or printer.
Hardware works with software to input, process, store and output data.
When asked for the collective term, write hardware rather than naming an individual component.
Types and components of computer systems

An internal printed circuit board.
Provides connections for the processor and other internal components.
Allows connected components to communicate with one another.
Describe the printed circuit board and its connections; calling it the “brain” is insufficient.
Types and components of computer systems

Controls the output sent to a monitor.
Processes graphics for display.
Has a graphics processing unit and its own memory.
Provides connections for display devices.
Types and components of computer systems

Handles sound input and output.
Receives sound input from a microphone.
Supports analogue-to-digital conversion when recording sound.
Supports digital-to-analogue conversion when playing sound through speakers.
Rewording the question does not explain how recording takes place.
Types and components of computer systems

NIC means Network Interface Card.
A hardware component or circuit board that connects a computer to a network.
Transmits and receives data over the network.
Controls the flow of network data.
Provides the device with a MAC address.
Enables communication and resource sharing with other networked devices.
Distinguish what a NIC is from what it does. Do not substitute the router’s role.
Types and components of computer systems

Software consists of programs or applications used by a computer.
Application software lets the user perform a task.
Examples include word processing, spreadsheets, database management and applets.
System software provides services needed for the computer to operate.
System software controls hardware and software and provides a platform for applications.
Examples include operating systems, compilers, linkers, device drivers and utilities.
Saying it is intangible or cannot be touched is insufficient; software is the programs, rather than something that runs programs.
Types and components of computer systems

A text editor used to create documents.
Allows users to type and edit text.
Allows text to be formatted.
Allows documents to be stored and printed.
Give generic application-software types rather than brand names.
Types and components of computer systems

Organises data in rows and columns.
Uses formulas to perform calculations.
Can display data using graphs.
Supports what-if modelling by changing input values.
Incorrect formulas can produce incorrect results.
A model may omit factors that affect the real situation.
Give generic application-software types rather than brand names.
Types and components of computer systems

Manages a collection of structured or organised data.
Stores data in fields, records and tables.
Allows records to be added, edited and corrected.
Allows data to be searched and retrieved.
Can produce reports.
Can store large amounts of data.
Give generic application-software types rather than brand names.
Types and components of computer systems

Control software manages or regulates external hardware.
Can change the environment through an automatic control system.
Receives sensor data and compares it with a preset value.
Sends a signal to an actuator when action is needed.
Measurement software allows a computer to interact with sensors.
Measurement software displays and helps analyse data about physical quantities.
Do not treat the sensor as the microprocessor or replace the requested processing explanation with sensor operation.
Types and components of computer systems

An app is software that helps a user carry out a specific task.
An applet is a small computer program.
An applet performs a specific task within a larger application.
Give generic application-software types rather than brand names.
Types and components of computer systems

Allows features to be added to sound.
Can generate sounds.
Can export sound.
Can edit track length, timing and volume.
Can combine tracks and apply fades or noise reduction.
Identify and explain an audio-editing feature.
Types and components of computer systems

Allows features to be added to a video.
Can arrange clips and add titles or sound.
Can adjust colour and apply effects or transitions.
Can output video in different file formats.
Allows video to be exported.
Describe specific editing operations, such as cropping, rather than saying the software “edits videos”.
Types and components of computer systems

A graphics editor is used to create or edit images.
Bitmap graphics are made from pixels.
Vector graphics use lines, curves and other defined objects.
The choice of editor depends on the type of image and the changes required.
Types and components of computer systems

CAD means Computer-Aided Design.
Helps users create 2D drawings and 3D models.
Creates digital representations of objects before they are manufactured.
Allows designs to be developed and modified.
Can support dimensions, different views and design analysis.
Types and components of computer systems

A type of system software.
Translates a program written in a high-level language into machine code.
The original program is source code.
The translated program is object code.
The compiled code can be used repeatedly without recompiling an unchanged program.
Give generic system-software examples, such as linkers and compilers.
Types and components of computer systems

A type of system software.
Combines one or more object files into a single executable program.
Allows separately written modules to be brought together.
Works with object files produced by a compiler.
Give generic system-software examples, such as linkers and compilers.
Types and components of computer systems

Software that enables a hardware device to communicate with the operating system.
A device needs an appropriate driver to work with the computer.
The operating system looks for a suitable driver when a device is connected.
Examples include drivers for printers and other peripherals.
Give generic system-software examples, such as linkers and compilers.
Types and components of computer systems

Utilities help manage, maintain and protect a computer system.
Antivirus software scans for known viruses and can use a database of virus signatures.
Anti-malware software detects and removes malicious software.
Infected files may be quarantined or deleted.
Protection software needs regular updates and scans.
Other utilities include backup, file management and disk maintenance tools.
Give precise prevention measures, including up-to-date antivirus and avoiding attachments from untrusted sources.
Types and components of computer systems

Analogue data is continuous.
Can take any value within a range.
Can be represented by a waveform.
Needs conversion to digital data before computer processing.
State analogue as the type of data output from the sensor.
Types and components of computer systems

Digital data is discrete.
Represented using binary values: 1s and 0s.
Can be processed by a computer without analogue-to-digital conversion.
Sampling can be used to obtain digital data from an analogue signal.
State digital as the data read by a microprocessor.
Types and components of computer systems

ADC means Analogue-to-Digital Converter.
Converts analogue data or signals into digital data.
Conversion is needed because computers process digital data.
Analogue input may come from sensors or microphones.
Used when recording sound or collecting analogue measurements.
Explain that analogue data must be converted for computer processing.
Types and components of computer systems

DAC means Digital-to-Analogue Converter.
Converts digital data or signals into analogue form.
Allows digital output to be used by analogue output devices.
Used in sound playback through speakers and in control systems with analogue outputs.
Explain that analogue output enables control of devices or can be sent to an actuator.
Types and components of computer systems

CPU means Central Processing Unit.
Fetches instructions and data from memory.
Decodes and executes instructions.
Performs calculations and logical operations.
Controls the transfer of data and instructions.
Microprocessors can be embedded in devices such as washing machines, cookers and alarms.
Explain technical processing steps. Instructions and data are fetched from memory, not directly from the user.
Types and components of computer systems

The Control Unit coordinates operations and the movement of data and instructions.
The Arithmetic and Logic Unit performs calculations, comparisons and logical operations.
Registers provide small areas of storage within the CPU for data, instructions or results being used.
These components work together during instruction processing.
“Brain of the computer” and general descriptions of the whole computer do not answer the question.
Types and components of computer systems

RAM means Random Access Memory.
Stores programs, instructions and data currently in use.
Can be read from and written to.
Stores data temporarily.
It is volatile: stored data is lost when power is removed.
It is primary storage directly accessed by the CPU.
Specify data and instructions currently in use. Volatile and losing data without power are the same characteristic.
Types and components of computer systems

ROM means Read-Only Memory.
Stores startup instructions.
May contain BIOS, hardware initialisation and self-test routines.
It is non-volatile: stored data is retained without power.
Stores data permanently.
Described as read-only in the course’s RAM/ROM comparison.
Do not confuse ROM with RAM or CD-ROM. Give distinct characteristics.
Types and components of computer systems

Similarity: both are internal memory.
Similarity: both are primary storage.
Similarity: the data on both can be read.
Similarity: both are directly accessed by the CPU.
Difference: RAM is volatile, whereas ROM is non-volatile.
Difference: RAM can be read from and written to, whereas ROM is read-only.
Difference: RAM stores data temporarily, whereas ROM stores data permanently.
Difference: RAM stores current programs and instructions, whereas ROM stores startup instructions.
Make direct, paired comparisons and do not reverse RAM and ROM characteristics.
Types and components of computer systems

BIOS means Basic Input/Output System.
Stored in ROM.
Carries out hardware checks when the computer starts.
Checks whether devices are present and working.
Loads the operating system into RAM.
Write ROM clearly and distinguish it from RAM.
Types and components of computer systems

CMOS means Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor.
Stores configuration information such as date, time and hardware settings in the textbook’s description.
A battery maintains these settings while the computer is switched off.
Types and components of computer systems

Sends data to a computer for processing.
Allows data or instructions to enter a system.
Manual input examples include a keyboard, mouse and touch screen.
Other examples include microphones, cameras, scanners and sensors.
Direct data-entry devices include barcode, QR, RFID, OMR and OCR readers.
Name a specific input device, not a computer category such as smartphone or tablet.
Types and components of computer systems

Receives data from the computer.
Communicates the results of processing.
Can display information, produce sound, print output or control a device.
Examples include monitors, printers, projectors, speakers and actuators.
Name a specific output device and match it to its function.
Types and components of computer systems
Devices with input and output functions

Some devices perform both input and output functions.
A touch screen displays information as output and detects touches as input.
A DVD writer/player can read stored data and write data to a disc.
Types and components of computer systems

Input devices send data to the computer
 output devices receive data from it.
Input allows data or instructions to be entered
 output communicates processing results or controls devices.
Both connect to a computer, handle data and use digital signals.
In the course comparison, input devices are controlled by the user and output devices by the computer.
Keep the direction of data flow clear: into the computer for input, from the computer for output.
Types and components of computer systems

Non-volatile storage used to retain data when power is removed.
Stores applications, the operating system and user files.
Generally has greater capacity and slower access than internal memory.
Examples include hard disks, SSDs, optical discs, magnetic tape and flash memory.
Also called secondary storage.
Types and components of computer systems

Fixed storage remains installed in the computer.
Removable storage can be taken out or disconnected.
Examples of removable storage include pen drives, memory cards and optical discs.
Portable external HDDs and SSDs can transfer or store files away from the computer.
Types and components of computer systems

A backup is a separate copy of data.
Used to restore data that has been lost, damaged or corrupted.
The backup can be stored securely away from the original.
Portable SSDs allow fast backup and restoration.
SSDs are robust and are not affected by magnetic fields.
Types and components of computer systems

Both internal memory and backing storage store data.
Internal memory is primary storage directly accessed by the CPU.
Backing storage is secondary storage.
Internal memory generally has faster access
 backing storage generally has greater capacity.
Internal memory may be volatile or non-volatile
 backing storage is non-volatile.
RAM holds current work, while backing storage retains files for later use.
Types and components of computer systems

System software that manages the computer’s basic operations.
Controls hardware and software.
Provides a link between the user and the hardware.
Provides a platform for other software to run.
Manages loading and running programs, files and storage.
Provides a user interface and security functions.
Explain that application software lets the user complete tasks, while system software operates the system or provides a platform for other software.
Types and components of computer systems

CLI means Command Line Interface.
Users type text commands.
Commands must use the correct syntax.
Users need to learn or remember commands.
Uses less memory and processing power than a graphical interface.
Experienced users can operate it quickly.
Explain what becomes faster for an expert user rather than writing only “faster”.
Types and components of computer systems

GUI means Graphical User Interface.
Users select graphical options rather than type command syntax.
Common elements are windows, icons, menus and a pointing device.
Can be easier for beginners to use.
Reduces command-typing errors and the need to learn complex syntax.
Can require significant RAM, storage space and processing power.
Do not confuse a graphical interface with a gesture-based interface.
Types and components of computer systems

WIMP means Windows, Icons, Menus and Pointing device.
Windows provide areas for displaying programs or documents.
Icons represent applications, files or actions.
Menus present options or commands.
A pointing device lets the user select on-screen items.
A window manager handles the arrangement of windows and pointer interaction.
Types and components of computer systems

Post-WIMP interaction goes beyond the traditional mouse-and-menu approach.
Touch-screen interaction can use pinching, zooming and rotating.
Can make selecting or manipulating displayed items quicker.
A touch interface can reduce the space needed for separate input devices.
Do not assume the small screen and typing limitations of a smartphone.
Types and components of computer systems

CLI uses typed commands
 GUI uses graphical options.
CLI users need to know command names and syntax
 GUI users can select visible options.
GUI is generally easier for beginners.
CLI can be quicker for experienced users.
CLI generally uses less memory and processing power than GUI.
Types and components of computer systems

Uses speech recognition to interact with the user.
Uses spoken words or voice to carry out actions or control devices.
Can use natural language processing to interpret and respond to commands.
Examples include voice-operated personal assistants.
Voice recognition may need training for the user’s voice.
Describe speech recognition and how spoken commands control actions.
Types and components of computer systems

Allows hands-free control.
Can help users who have difficulty using a keyboard or mouse.
Can speed up data entry.
Background noise, accents or speech difficulties can affect recognition.
Commands may need to be learnt and spoken clearly.
The system may have a limited set of recognised commands.
Comparisons with CLI, costs, controlling the vehicle, or claims that a satellite must be present miss the required focus.
Types and components of computer systems

Uses body movement as input.
Cameras, sensors or trackers detect movements.
The system interprets recognised movements as commands.
Can control a device without a keyboard, mouse or physical contact.
Used in interactive games and other movement-controlled systems.
Explain detection and interpretation of body movements; saying “uses gestures” repeats the topic.
Types and components of computer systems

Can provide natural, contactless interaction.
Can make games feel more realistic.
Movements must be demonstrated clearly and recognised accurately.
Accidental movements can trigger commands.
Lighting, distance from the camera and available space can affect use.
Repeated movements can cause fatigue.
Some users may be unable to perform the required gestures.
Relate limitations to movement recognition, accidental activation and the user’s ability to perform gestures.
Types and components of computer systems

Typically has separate components such as a monitor and keyboard.
Can be customised and expanded by changing components or peripherals.
Normally uses mains power.
Often provides high storage capacity and processing performance.
Has a relatively large footprint and is less portable.
Used for office work, education, gaming and entertainment.
A larger screen or keyboard needs its effect explained; “tablets are more portable” is clearer than an absolute claim that desktops are not portable.
Types and components of computer systems

Laptops are mobile, lighter and have a smaller footprint.
Laptop components are integrated and laptops can run on batteries.
Desktops are easier to expand or repair using standard components.
Laptops can be more difficult or expensive to repair.
Desktops often provide more stable wired connectivity and better heat dissipation.
Desktops require mains power and may have more trailing cables.
Give developed differences between laptops and desktops, particularly portability.
Types and components of computer systems

Mobile computers can be carried and used in different places.
Categories include laptops, smartphones, tablets and phablets.
Hybrid devices combine features of different categories.
Give mobile computers rather than phones.
Types and components of computer systems

A portable computer with integrated components.
Has a screen and physical keyboard.
Can run from a battery or mains electricity.
Has a smaller footprint than a desktop.
Can provide more comfortable typing and a larger screen than a smartphone.
Common uses include work, education and entertainment.
Do not switch to other inputs such as images.
Types and components of computer systems

Portable, so work and stored data can move between locations.
A physical keyboard and larger screen can help with typing and checking work.
Ports make connecting peripherals and transferring data easier.
Can be lost, stolen or damaged in transit.
Battery life can limit use away from power.
Personal storage devices or downloads can introduce malware or security risks.
Do not switch to other inputs such as images.
Types and components of computer systems

Combines mobile communication with computing applications.
Common built-in devices include a camera, microphone, touch screen, speaker and display.
Can connect through mobile networks, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.
Supports calls, messaging and video calls.
Can use existing networks for online communication.
Signal loss, lag and a small screen can limit communication.
Explain that smartphones depend on land-based towers that may be unavailable there.
Types and components of computer systems

A proximity sensor detects when the phone is close to the user’s ear.
Proximity detection helps prevent unintended touches.
An accelerometer detects movement and orientation.
Orientation sensing can change a display between portrait and landscape.
Speech recognition allows voice-based commands and searches.
Types and components of computer systems

OLED means Organic Light Emitting Diode.
The textbook discusses OLED touch screens in relation to thinner, lighter smartphones.
Li-Fi communicates using visible light rather than radio waves.
The textbook presents solar-assisted OLED displays and Li-Fi as possible developments, rather than standard features of every smartphone.
Types and components of computer systems

Small and lightweight, so easy to carry.
Often available when a separate computer is not.
Supports mobile internet, calls and built-in camera or microphone use.
A small screen and small controls can make work difficult.
Battery power, storage and software compatibility can limit use.
Movement or unreliable connections can interrupt calls or online activity.
Notifications and other phone functions can distract the user.
Do not switch to other inputs such as images.
Types and components of computer systems

A mobile computer with a touch-screen interface.
Usually uses an on-screen keyboard, with a physical keyboard possible on some models.
Can have cameras, a microphone and other sensors.
Portable and has a small footprint.
Touch selection can make interaction easier.
Typing may be less convenient without an external keyboard.
Battery life and the risk of loss or damage are limitations.
A larger screen or keyboard needs its effect explained; “tablets are more portable” is clearer than an absolute claim that desktops are not portable.
Types and components of computer systems

Tablets are generally easy to carry and use through a touch screen.
Laptops provide a physical keyboard that is useful for extended typing.
Software availability and compatibility influence the choice.
Storage capacity, ports and file transfer can differ.
Battery life, heat, startup and standby behaviour are relevant comparisons.
Choose according to the task rather than assuming one device is always better.
Types and components of computer systems

A hybrid of a smartphone and tablet.
Provides smartphone functions in a tablet-like device.
Its size lies between a smartphone and a tablet in the textbook comparison.
A larger screen makes content easier to see than on a smaller phone.
A larger on-screen keyboard can reduce typing errors.
Larger size makes it less portable or less convenient for one-handed use.
Use the precise term smartphone rather than the ambiguous “phone”.
Types and components of computer systems
Uses of smartphones, tablets and phablets

Calls, messaging, email and video communication.
Internet access, social networking and online banking.
Photography, audio and video recording.
Games and other entertainment.
Education, business tasks and calendar management.
Navigation and location-based services.
Remote control of connected devices.
Explain consequences: a small screen limits visibility; integrated peripherals reduce extra purchases.
Types and components of computer systems

AI means Artificial Intelligence.
Computer systems simulate aspects of human intelligence.
Can mimic problem solving, decision making or behaviour.
Can learn from previous decisions.
Applications include language processing, image recognition and autonomous systems.
Explain what AI does rather than listing devices that use it.
Types and components of computer systems

Analyses large amounts of data.
Can personalise recommendations, services and search results.
Can learn and adapt to users’ needs.
Can recognise faces or identify unwanted material.
Can support decision making, safety and product or service quality.
Robotic systems can undertake dangerous or unpleasant work.
Distinguish AI from AR and VR; lengthy comments on image enhancement alone miss the required concept.
Types and components of computer systems

Automation can replace some tasks previously done by people.
Some jobs may be lost, while new technical roles may be created.
Dependence on technology can reduce human skills.
AI can collect and analyse substantial personal information.
Personalisation can influence user choices and raise privacy or security concerns.
Types and components of computer systems

Asimov’s laws are fictional rules for robots, not a statement of how all real robots operate.
A robot must not injure a human, or allow a human to be harmed through inaction.
A robot must obey human orders unless they conflict with the first law.
A robot must protect itself unless doing so conflicts with the first two laws.
Types and components of computer systems

XR means Extended Reality.
An umbrella term covering Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality and Mixed Reality.
Combines or connects aspects of the physical and digital worlds.
Different XR technologies vary in how much of the real world remains visible.
Explain extended reality using both VR and AR.
Types and components of computer systems

Combines virtual content with a view of the real world.
Adds a digital layer over existing reality.
Can display information about real objects or surroundings.
Can be accessed using a smartphone or suitable glasses.
The real-world setting remains part of the experience.
State and develop differences between AR and VR.
Types and components of computer systems

Can display information or warnings over a real scene.
Used in gaming, social-media filters and immersive learning.
Can help shoppers view information or try products virtually.
Used in healthcare and other tasks requiring information overlaid on a view.
On-screen information can distract the user.
Immersion in an AR activity can create safety or social-interaction risks.
Name AR uses clearly, such as gaming, education or military applications.
Types and components of computer systems

Creates a completely computer-generated environment.
Can use a headset or goggles.
Provides an immersive view of a simulated world.
Can give the user a 360-degree experience.
The user’s view is primarily of the virtual environment rather than the real surroundings.
State and develop differences between AR and VR.
Types and components of computer systems

Used in games, walkthroughs and training systems.
Allows repeated practice in a virtual environment.
Can support training without exposing people to real danger.
Allows designs to be explored and errors found before implementation.
Can provide an interactive experience and improve retention.
Can cause headaches, eyestrain, motion sickness or disorientation.
Users may confuse virtual activity with real life or become over-dependent on gaming.
Give other uses of VR; gaming was a common credited response.
Types and components of computer systems

AR overlays digital content on a real-world setting.
VR provides a completely computer-generated environment.
AR can be accessed using a smartphone, while VR commonly uses a headset.
AR preserves a view of the real surroundings
 VR immerses the user in a simulated world.
State and develop differences between AR and VR.

A keyboard is a manual input device used to enter characters and commands.
Pressing a key completes a circuit in a membrane or circuit board.
The computer identifies the key and interprets its character code.
Connects by USB or wirelessly; some devices use an on-screen keyboard.
Name the actual input device, rather than a computer type.

Enters text into word processors and other applications.
Enters numbers into spreadsheets and database fields.
Enters commands, passwords and keyboard shortcuts.
A physical keyboard is suitable for typing large amounts of text.
Keep typing benefits linked to entering text, rather than switching to image input.

A familiar method that allows rapid text entry for a skilled typist.
Typed data can be checked against the source as it is entered.
A larger physical keyboard can make typing easier and reduce entry errors.
Manual typing is slower than direct data entry and can introduce errors.
Occupies desk space and can be difficult for users with restricted hand movement.
Explain how a larger physical keyboard helps typing or reduces entry errors.

Repeated keyboard use can cause repetitive strain injury (RSI) in hands or wrists.
Ergonomic keyboards arrange keys to support a more natural hand position.
Wrist and hand support can reduce strain during typing.
An ergonomic keyboard addresses RSI; an anti-glare screen addresses eyestrain.
Distinguish RSI from eyestrain and back or neck problems.

A numeric keypad mainly enters numbers and a small set of function keys.
Each key press sends an input signal identifying the selected key.
Can be separate, built into a keyboard or displayed on a touch screen.

Enters PINs and withdrawal amounts at ATMs.
Enters PINs on chip and PIN terminals.
Enters product numbers when barcode scanning fails.
Enters telephone numbers and numeric spreadsheet data.

Can enter numeric data faster than a standard keyboard.
A small keypad is portable and occupies little space.
Small keys can make accurate entry difficult.
Different number layouts may confuse users.
Limited character entry makes it unsuitable for lengthy text.

A mouse is a pointing device that controls an on-screen pointer.
Moving an optical mouse changes the pointer position using detected reflected light.
Buttons select items or open context menus.
A scroll wheel moves through documents or pages.
Can connect by cable or wirelessly.

Selects icons, menu options and links.
Opens, closes and moves application windows.
Selects, moves and deletes files.
Supports drawing, image editing and drag-and-drop operations.

Quick selection of visible options compared with keyboard navigation.
Convenient for moving through applications and web pages.
Usually needs a suitable flat surface and space to move.
May be difficult for users with restricted hand or wrist movement.
Mechanical ball mice can collect dirt, reducing accurate movement.

A touchpad is a touch-sensitive pointing surface, commonly built into a laptop.
Moving a finger controls the pointer.
Tapping or pressing buttons selects items.
Gestures can provide scrolling and other actions.

Selects icons and menu options on a laptop.
Navigates applications and web pages.
Moves files or objects using drag-and-drop.
Provides pointing input without a separate mouse.

Built into the laptop, so no separate mouse needs carrying.
Does not need an additional flat surface for mouse movement.
Allows quick selection of on-screen options.
Accurate pointer control and drag-and-drop can be harder than with a mouse.
Can be difficult for users with restricted hand movement.

A trackerball is a stationary pointing device with a ball on its top or side.
The user rotates the ball to move the pointer.
Buttons select items in a similar way to mouse buttons.
The whole device does not need to move across the desk.

An alternative to a mouse for users with limited wrist movement.
Selects options in industrial control rooms.
Controls functions in some in-car entertainment and navigation systems.

Requires less desk space because the device stays stationary.
Can be easier for users with limited hand or wrist movement.
Can provide accurate pointer positioning without moving the whole arm.
May cost extra because it is not normally supplied as standard.
Users unfamiliar with the device may need practice or training.

A remote control sends commands to another device.
Buttons select functions such as volume, channel or power.
The textbook describes infrared transmission between remote and receiver.
The receiving device interprets the transmitted command.

Controls televisions, audio systems and media players.
Controls multimedia presentation equipment.
Starts, stops or changes industrial processes from a distance.

Allows equipment to be controlled without approaching it.
Can keep an operator away from hazardous machinery.
Infrared signals can be blocked by obstacles and have limited range.
Small buttons can be difficult for users with restricted hand movement.

A joystick is a movable stick used to control direction or movement.
Sensors detect the stick position.
Buttons provide additional commands or selections.
The computer uses these signals to move an on-screen object.

Controls movement in computer games.
Provides realistic control in flight and other simulators.
Allows directional control using a single hand-operated stick.

Can provide more realistic control than a keyboard in suitable games or simulations.
Directional movement can be easier than using separate keys.
Precise pointer positioning can be harder than with a mouse.
Its suitability depends on the application being controlled.

A driving wheel is an input device that simulates a vehicle steering wheel.
Sensors detect left and right rotation.
Pedals or buttons provide braking, acceleration and other controls.
Usually connects to a computer or console through USB.

Controls steering in racing games.
Used with driving simulators to practise vehicle control.
Works with pedals to simulate acceleration and braking.

Steering movements are more natural than keyboard commands.
Can provide a more realistic driving experience.
Can cost more than a mouse or joystick.
Over-sensitive steering can feel unrealistic.
Basic models may provide little or no force feedback.
Touch screens (as an input device): characteristics and operation

A touch screen detects where the user touches its surface.
Touching an icon or button enters a selection without a separate pointing device.
Can support gestures such as pinch and zoom.
The same screen can provide input and display output.
Distinguish detecting a touch from displaying the output.
Touch screens (as an input device): uses

Selects options at ATMs and self-service tills.
Provides menus at restaurant point-of-sale terminals.
Used in public information kiosks and satellite navigation.
Used in smartphones, tablets and interactive classroom displays.
Touch screens (as an input device): advantages and disadvantages

Allows quick, direct selection of on-screen options.
Combines display and pointing input, reducing the footprint of separate devices.
Supports gestures such as pinch and zoom.
Repeated reaching can strain arm muscles.
Dirt can reduce responsiveness, and damage can make input difficult.
Explain the effect of a feature rather than claiming only that it is easier.
Explain what becomes quicker or easier; do not assume every touch screen has a smartphone-sized display.

A scanner captures a digital image of a physical document or photograph.
A flatbed scanner illuminates the document placed on its glass.
Reflected light is detected and converted into digital image data.
OCR software is needed to turn scanned text images into editable characters.
A scanned text image is not editable text until OCR has recognised the characters.

Digitises printed photographs and illustrations.
Captures paper documents for storage or archiving.
Provides text images for OCR processing.
Scanned images can be edited using graphics software.

Captures detailed digital images of flat documents.
Avoids photographing a document at an angle, which can distort its shape.
Both scanners and digital cameras capture and store digital images.
A scanner is generally less portable than a digital camera.
Scanning text alone does not make that text editable.
Make paired camera–scanner comparisons rather than two unrelated descriptions.

A digital camera captures photographs as digital image data.
Light reaches an electronic image sensor through a lens.
Images are stored in internal memory or on a memory card.
Captured images can be transferred to a computer.

Captures photographs for documents, websites and publications.
Records images at locations away from a computer.
Provides image input for communication or identification systems.
Can capture moving images if video recording is supported.

Portable and can capture images quickly.
Images can be viewed, deleted and transferred without developing film.
Both a camera and scanner create digital images.
Photographing a printed page can introduce glare, shadows or perspective distortion.
A scanner can capture a flat document in greater detail.
Compare the camera with the specified alternative and account for glare, shadows and image distortion.

Connect the camera or storage device to the computer using a USB cable.
Transfer wirelessly using Bluetooth where supported.
Use Wi-Fi to transfer images or download them from cloud storage.
A memory card can be read using a compatible card reader.
Name the transfer method; cloud storage alone is not a transfer method.
Name cable, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi; cloud storage alone does not describe the transfer.

Both can capture and store digital photographs.
A smartphone is often already available and can share images through its network connection.
A dedicated camera may provide optical zoom, interchangeable lenses or more manual controls.
Image quality depends on the model, lens and sensor rather than device category alone.
Choose according to portability, required image quality and available controls.

A microphone is an input device that captures sound.
Converts sound vibrations into an electrical signal.
Analogue sound data is converted into digital data by an ADC or sound card.
The computer can process or store the resulting digital audio.
Describe capture, analogue-to-digital conversion and computer storage rather than repeating the question.

Records speech, music and other sounds.
Captures participants' voices during audio or video conferences.
Provides input for speech recognition and voice commands.
Can supply analogue sound data to an ADC.
Microphones capture sound; webcams capture images.

Allows speech and sound to be entered without typing.
Useful for voice control and hands-free interaction.
Background noise can interfere with recordings or speech recognition.
Sound quality depends on microphone position and recording conditions.
Voice input can be difficult for users with speech difficulties.

Sensors measure physical quantities and supply data to a computer system.
Many sensors produce analogue data that needs conversion by an ADC.
Monitoring systems collect or display readings, often continuously or at regular intervals.
Control systems compare readings with preset values and signal actuators when needed.
A sensor measures; the processor makes the programmed comparison and control decision.
Separate the sensor’s measurement from the processor’s comparison and the actuator’s action.

Measures temperature in heating and air-conditioning systems.
Monitors temperature in greenhouses or industrial processes.
Collects temperature readings in weather monitoring.
Can form part of a security or fire-detection system.
Use the sensor name, not a general device name such as thermometer.
Name a temperature sensor; thermometer is a device name rather than the required sensor name.

Measures pressure in industrial processes or fluid systems.
Pressure pads can detect a person or object in a security system.
Can detect an athlete leaving a starting block.
Collects atmospheric pressure data in weather monitoring.

Measures light intensity.
Controls lighting in response to ambient light levels.
Monitors light for plant-growing systems.
Detects interruption of a light beam, such as at a race finish or security boundary.

Detects sound or measures sound level.
Can detect a starting pistol to begin race timing.
Monitors noise levels.
Can detect unexpected sounds in a security system.

A humidity sensor measures moisture in air.
A moisture sensor can measure water content in soil.
Used to monitor greenhouse conditions and control irrigation.
Used in weather-monitoring systems.
Choose the sensor according to what is being measured; do not count moisture and humidity twice when treated as the same answer.
Do not give moisture and humidity as two separate answers when they are treated as equivalent.

Measures acidity or alkalinity.
Monitors pH in rivers and other water supplies.
Checks conditions in chemical or industrial processes.
Can provide feedback for controlling the pH of a solution.

Collects data automatically without repeated manual entry.
Can collect continuously or at regular intervals, including 24 hours a day.
Can reduce human data-entry errors and improve measurement accuracy.
Allows readings to be collected from hazardous or inaccessible locations.
Faulty or dirty sensors can produce incorrect results.
Installation, maintenance and environmental conditions can create difficulties or extra costs.
Develop benefits and drawbacks of data collection rather than describing only how the sensor works.

A light pen is a pointing input device described for use with compatible CRT screens.
A light detector in the pen detects light from the screen.
The system determines the selected screen position from the detected signal.
It does not operate like a normal pen writing on paper.

Selects objects directly on a compatible screen.
Can be used for drawing or computer-aided design.
Provides direct interaction with screen positions without moving a separate mouse.

Allows direct and potentially accurate selection on the screen.
Needs little desk space for a separate pointing surface.
Must be used with compatible display technology.
Holding the pen against a screen for long periods can strain the arm.
May obscure part of the displayed image while selecting it.

Direct data entry captures data without a person retyping it.
Readers and scanners transfer encoded or recognised data to a computer.
Examples include barcode readers, QR scanners, RFID readers, OMR and OCR systems.
A keyboard or mouse is a manual input device rather than direct data entry.
Name the reader or scanner, not only the code, card or tag.
Name the reader or scanner. Keyboard and mouse are not direct data-entry devices.
Magnetic stripe readers: characteristics and operation

Reads data stored magnetically on a stripe.
The card is swiped through the reader so the stripe passes the reading head.
The reader converts the encoded magnetic data into computer input.
Physical contact can cause wear on the card or reader.
Compare the readers, not just the cards.

Reads identification or account details from magnetic-stripe cards.
Used in access-control and membership systems.
Can be used to input card information for payment systems that support magnetic stripes.
Magnetic stripe readers: advantages and disadvantages

Quickly reads stored data without manual typing.
The stripe has to pass through the reader correctly.
Stripe damage or wear can prevent reliable reading.
In the textbook comparison, a stripe-only transaction does not require a PIN, making misuse easier than chip and PIN.
Magnetic-stripe and chip readers both make physical contact with the card.
Explain why a PIN improves security rather than stating only that a system is more secure.
Contactless debit card readers: characteristics and operation

A compatible contactless reader communicates with a card over a short distance.
Uses radio-based near-field communication.
The reader obtains the payment data when the card is held close.
The card does not need to be swiped or inserted.

Makes contactless credit or debit card payments.
Used at supported checkout and transport payment terminals.
Inputs card-payment information by holding a compatible card near the reader.
Contactless debit card readers: advantages and disadvantages

Can complete suitable payments quickly without inserting the card.
Avoids wear from repeatedly swiping or inserting a card.
Works only over a short distance with compatible equipment.
Security checks or transaction limits can require another verification step.
A lost card can pose a risk if used before it is blocked.
Chip and PIN readers: characteristics and operation

Reads data from the embedded chip when a card is inserted.
Prompts the customer to enter a PIN using a keypad.
The system checks the entered PIN before authorising the transaction.
The card and reader make physical contact.
The chip is read by the reader; the keypad is used to enter the PIN.

Used at shops and other businesses to authorise card payments.
Reads account information from the card's chip.
Allows the customer to enter their PIN to verify the transaction.
Chip and PIN readers: advantages and disadvantages

A PIN adds security compared with the textbook's stripe-only transaction.
Requires the user to know and enter the correct PIN.
Entering a PIN can take longer than a stripe-only transaction.
A person watching the keypad may obtain the PIN through shoulder surfing.
Contact can cause wear on the card or reader.
Support security comparisons with the need to know the PIN.
Radio frequency identification (RFID) readers: characteristics and operation

RFID means Radio Frequency Identification.
A reader sends radio waves to a tag or microchip.
A passive tag is activated by the reader's signal.
The tag returns encoded data by radio, which the reader reads.
Does not require optical line of sight.
Some systems can read multiple tags at the same time.
State that the reader activates the microchip using radio waves and receives its returned data.

Tracks stock, library books, livestock or event attendees.
Records race timings using tagged participants.
Reads implanted pet identification microchips.
Used in compatible contactless payment and identification systems.
State the specific tracking or identification purpose rather than only a location.
Give a specific purpose, such as tracking library books, rather than only naming a location.
Radio frequency identification (RFID) readers: advantages and disadvantages

Can read without optical line of sight and may read multiple tags together.
Can read tags from a distance appropriate to the system.
Tags can remain readable when their surface is defaced, provided the chip is not severely damaged.
Implanted pet tags are difficult to lose and suffer little wear.
Readers and tags add cost and create reliance on working equipment.
RFID still requires reading or scanning; it is not a system with no scanning.
RFID tags still have to be read or scanned. Lack of optical line of sight does not mean no reading takes place.
Optical mark recognition/reader (OMR): characteristics and operation

OMR means Optical Mark Recognition.
Detects marks in predefined positions on a form.
A reader uses optical detection to identify marked areas.
Software interprets the positions as selected responses.
Does not recognise the written characters themselves.
Explain detection of marks in predefined positions; do not confuse OMR with recognising characters.

Reads multiple-choice answer sheets.
Reads questionnaires and surveys with marked options.
Processes suitable lottery forms or tickets.
Reads attendance forms with predefined marking positions.
Use precise examples such as multiple-choice answer sheets rather than the vague phrase marking exams.
Optical mark recognition/reader (OMR): advantages and disadvantages

Inputs large numbers of marked responses quickly without retyping.
Predefined positions make automatic processing possible.
Marks must be made in the correct locations.
Poorly completed or damaged forms can produce reading errors.
Does not read free-form written characters in the way OCR does.
Explain the required mark positions rather than simply repeating the word marks.
Optical character recognition/reader (OCR): characteristics and operation

OCR means Optical Character Recognition.
Software recognises characters in a scanned or photographed image.
Converts the image of text into editable character data.
Can be used with a scanner or camera, but is distinct from capturing the image.
Recognised text can be used in word-processing software.
Distinguish OCR character recognition from scanning an image and from OMR.

Converts printed documents into editable text.
Inputs text without manually retyping the whole document.
Reads characters on vehicle number plates in ANPR systems.
In ANPR, the image is processed, characters are recognised and the result can be checked against a database.
In ANPR, describe image capture, character recognition and database checking; the camera alone does not do all processing.
Optical character recognition/reader (OCR): advantages and disadvantages

Reduces manual typing and can speed up text entry.
Can improve data entry compared with retyping, when the text is clear.
Unclear characters, inconsistent fonts or stray marks may be misinterpreted.
Recognised text must be checked and corrected.
In ANPR, dirt, obstructions, poor light or unusual fonts can prevent accurate reading.
OCR output needs proofreading because unclear or stray marks can be misread.

Both use optical methods to input data from printed documents.
Both support direct data entry and can process large amounts of data quickly.
OMR identifies marks in fixed positions, while OCR recognises characters.
OMR needs correctly located marks; OCR produces text that can be edited.
OCR errors require checking and correction of the recognised text.
Make direct comparisons explaining what each method recognises and how its result is used.

A barcode reader reads the pattern of contrasting bars and spaces.
Uses light and detects the reflected pattern.
Converts the pattern into a code sent to the computer.
The code can identify a record in a database.
Conventional barcode reading requires a suitable optical view of the code.
Name a barcode reader or scanner, not a barcode.

Scans product codes at a checkout.
The computer searches the stock database using the code.
A sale reduces the recorded stock quantity.
The system compares the quantity with a reorder level and can request new stock.
Stock records are updated when deliveries arrive.
Also supports tracking items through a system.
Connect scanning to database lookup, stock reduction, comparison with the reorder level and updating new stock.

Scans codes faster than typing their numbers.
Reduces manual data-entry errors.
Damaged, folded or missing codes may not be readable.
Incorrectly assigned codes are not automatically recognised as wrong.
Requires scanner hardware and working software.
Compared with RFID, optical barcodes need line of sight and are generally read individually.
Compare with typing the code and explain both reduced entry errors and unreadable or incorrect codes.
Quick response (QR) code scanners (readers): characteristics and operation

A QR code is a two-dimensional pattern encoding data.
A camera captures the pattern and suitable QR-reading software decodes it.
Can be read from different orientations.
Can encode information such as a website address.
The input device is a QR code reader or scanner, not the code itself.
Name a QR reader or scanner; a code alone is not an input device.

Provides links to product information or websites.
Tracks stock or identifies items.
Gives access to instructions or other encoded information.
Can be read using a camera-equipped device with suitable software.
Explain camera capture and suitable decoding software rather than saying only use a phone.
Quick response (QR) code scanners (readers): advantages and disadvantages

Can store more information than a conventional one-dimensional barcode.
Can be read from several angles.
A small printed code can save space on packaging.
Can link directly to further information.
Needs suitable image capture and decoding software.
Poor image quality or severe damage can prevent reading.
Link each benefit to the application, such as more information or less packaging space.

A conventional barcode encodes data in one dimension; a QR code uses a two-dimensional pattern.
QR codes can hold more information, including website addresses.
QR codes can be read in different orientations.
Both require a suitable reader and decoding process.
A QR code can be read by a camera with suitable software rather than a dedicated laser reader.

CRT means Cathode Ray Tube.
An electron gun directs beams towards a phosphor-coated screen.
The beams scan the screen and the phosphor emits light.
Different colour phosphors combine to form the displayed image.

Displays computer output such as text, images and video.
Historically used as computer monitors and television displays.
Can be used where an existing compatible CRT system is retained.

Can provide good colour reproduction and viewing angles.
Large and heavy compared with flat-panel displays.
Consumes more power and produces more heat than comparable LCD screens.
Occupies substantial desk space.
Flicker can contribute to eyestrain.

An LED-backlit LCD uses LEDs to illuminate a liquid-crystal display.
OLED means Organic Light Emitting Diode.
OLED pixels emit their own light and do not need a separate backlight.
OLED can produce very dark blacks and thin displays.
An LED-backlit LCD and an OLED display are different technologies.

LCD means Liquid Crystal Display.
Liquid crystals control how much light passes through each pixel.
A backlight supplies the light.
Colour filters and controlled subpixels form the image.
Commonly used in flat-panel monitors and portable displays.

Displays text, images and video on computers.
Used in laptops, tablets and other portable devices.
Used for televisions, information screens and other flat displays.

Thin and lightweight compared with CRT displays.
Uses less desk space and generally consumes less power than a CRT.
Produces less heat than a comparable CRT.
Viewing angle, colour reproduction and response time depend on the display.
A damaged panel can be expensive to replace.

LCD screens can use LED or cold-cathode fluorescent lamp (CCFL) backlighting.
LED backlighting generally uses less power.
LED systems can produce thinner displays and less heat.
LEDs can improve brightness control and contrast.
OLED is self-emitting and is not another name for LED backlighting.
Touch screen (as an output device): characteristics and operation

As an output device, a touch screen displays information like a flat-panel monitor.
The display presents buttons, icons, text and images.
Its touch-sensitive layer provides the separate input function.
A touch screen therefore performs both input and output roles.
Touch screen (as an output device): uses

Displays menus and transaction details at ATMs or self-service tills.
Displays information at public kiosks.
Shows applications, messages and media on tablets or smartphones.
Displays interactive teaching or training material.
Touch screen (as an output device): advantages and disadvantages

Combines a display with direct selection, reducing separate-device footprint.
Supports quick option selection and pinch-and-zoom interaction.
Repeated touching can leave dirt and reduce responsiveness.
Frequent reaching can strain arm muscles.
Damage can affect both display use and input.
Describe output as displaying information, not detecting a touch.

A multimedia projector displays computer or video output on a large surface.
Receives an image or video signal from a source device.
Uses a light source and projection optics to form an enlarged image.
Sound may need separate speakers or an integrated speaker.
Choose an output device appropriate to the required information.

Shows presentations to an audience.
Displays teaching material in classrooms.
Projects films, videos and demonstration screens.
Allows a group to view one computer's output.

Provides a large image that many people can see.
Avoids requiring every viewer to have a separate display.
Image visibility can be reduced by bright ambient light.
Needs a suitable projection surface and positioning.
People or objects can obstruct the beam.
Light sources and other components may need maintenance.

A laser printer is a non-impact page printer.
A laser forms an electrostatic image on a photosensitive drum.
Toner is attracted to the charged image.
Toner transfers to paper and is fixed by heat and pressure.
Produces hard-copy output.
Distinguish a laser printer from inkjet, dot matrix and 3D printing.

Prints high volumes of documents.
Used for reports, letters and office paperwork.
Suitable for fast production of high-quality text.
Can produce colour output when the printer supports it.

Produces high-quality hard copy and can print pages quickly.
Often suitable for large print volumes.
Initial equipment cost can be high.
Toner and maintenance create running costs.
Uses toner rather than the ink used by plotters and inkjet printers.
Can emit ozone; ventilation and equipment design affect exposure.
Compare hard-copy output directly and distinguish toner from ink.

An inkjet printer is a non-impact printer.
A moving print head sprays tiny droplets of ink onto paper.
Droplets form the text or image.
Uses ink cartridges or tanks.
Produces two-dimensional hard-copy output.
Inkjet printing forms a flat image using ink droplets; 3D printing builds a solid object.

Prints colour photographs and images.
Prints documents at home or in small offices.
Suitable for modest print volumes.
Can print on supported media such as photographic paper.

Can produce high-quality colour and photographic output.
Often has a lower purchase cost than a laser printer.
Ink replacement can be expensive for frequent printing.
Ink may smudge before drying or fade with time.
Often slower than a laser printer for large document runs.
Unlike a 3D printer, produces a flat image rather than a solid object.
Give differences when requested, rather than substituting similarities.
Inkjet droplet production: thermal bubble and piezoelectric

Thermal inkjet heats ink to create a bubble that forces a droplet through a nozzle.
Piezoelectric inkjet applies voltage to a crystal that changes shape.
The crystal's movement forces ink out of the nozzle.
Both methods control tiny ink droplets to build the image.
Dot matrix printers: characteristics and operation

A dot matrix printer is an impact printer.
Pins strike an inked ribbon against paper.
Patterns of dots form characters and images.
A moving print head builds up the printed output.

Produces multipart forms and carbon copies.
Used for invoices, receipts or industrial records where impact printing is useful.
Can print on continuous stationery.
Dot matrix printers: advantages and disadvantages

Impact printing can produce several copies through multipart paper.
Can work with continuous stationery.
Can be robust in suitable working environments.
Noisy compared with non-impact printers.
Lower print quality and generally slower output.
Not suitable for high-quality colour photographs.

A plotter produces accurate, large-format drawings or graphics.
Traditional pen plotters move pens relative to the drawing surface.
Other large-format plotters use ink-based printing mechanisms.
Produces hard copy and can work on supported large sheets or other materials.
A plotter is not a 3D printer.
A plotter produces drawings or graphics; it is not restricted to graphs and is not a 3D printer.

Produces architectural plans.
Produces engineering drawings and CAD output.
Prints maps and large-format graphics.
Can produce accurate drawings on different supported materials.
Link the output to the task, such as architectural drawings.

Can work on larger sheets than typical office printers.
Produces accurate, high-quality drawings.
Can use multiple colours and different supported materials.
Has a large footprint and is less portable.
Can be expensive to maintain and may be noisy.
Some plotting tasks take longer than page printing.
Develop benefits and drawbacks with the required drawing task in mind.

A 3D printer creates a solid object from a digital design.
Adds material in successive layers.
The material and process depend on the printer.
Examples include plastics, resins, metals or suitable specialist mixtures.
Unlike an inkjet printer, creates a three-dimensional object rather than a flat image.
Describe successive layers using material appropriate to the object.

Produces prototypes and manufactured components.
Creates customised prosthetics.
Produces surgical or diagnostic aids and medical tools.
Can create models of organs for practice.
Suitable specialist processes can make customised tablets, tissue structures or artificial blood vessels.
Give additional uses without repeating an example already supplied in the question.

Can make customised objects and reuse stored designs.
Can reduce material waste and the number of separate components.
Some production processes can be quicker or cheaper than conventional manufacture.
Printer size and supported materials limit the objects produced.
Equipment and skilled operation can have high initial costs.
Printing may take a long time, and design or printing errors can be difficult to correct.
Qualify speed and cost claims, and remember that accuracy depends on the design and program.

Direct 3D printing deposits material through a nozzle in layers.
Binder printing uses a binding substance to join powder particles.
Light-based methods cure or solidify suitable resin using light.
The printer repeats its process over successive layers.
The material and method must suit the object, such as a specialist mixture for a medicinal tablet.
Choose the printing material and process appropriate to the scenario.

Create or obtain a digital 3D model.
Prepare the design for printing and divide it into layers.
Set up the printer with the required material.
Print successive layers to build the solid object.
Remove supports or finish the object where required.
Check the design and settings because errors affect the resulting object.
Explain how repeated layers build the object rather than only naming the printer.

Speakers are output devices that produce sound.
A computer reads digital audio and sends it to a DAC or sound card.
The digital signal is converted to an analogue signal.
The signal drives the speaker to produce sound.
A microphone captures sound; a speaker outputs it.
Describe digital-to-analogue conversion and the signal sent to the speakers.

Plays recorded speech, music and sound effects.
Lets conference participants hear other people.
Provides audible warnings or announcements.
Can provide sound output in control systems such as pedestrian crossings.
Speakers let users hear sound; microphones capture it.

Communicates audio without requiring the user to read a display.
Useful for music, speech and warning signals.
Sound can disturb other people or be masked by background noise.
Public sound output offers little privacy.
May not meet the needs of users with hearing impairments without an alternative output.

An actuator is an output device that produces a physical action.
Receives a control signal from a computer or microprocessor.
May operate a motor, valve, heater or other mechanism.
A processor compares sensor data with a preset value and signals the actuator when action is required.
The sensor supplies readings; the actuator carries out the action.
The processor compares readings with a preset value; the actuator performs the physical action.

Opens or closes greenhouse windows.
Applies brakes in an automatic braking system.
Operates valves or pumps in a control system.
Drives motors or switches equipment on and off as instructed by a controller.
State the action, such as opening greenhouse windows or applying brakes.

Carries out programmed actions automatically and repeatedly.
Can respond quickly to control signals.
Can perform actions in hazardous or inaccessible locations.
Mechanical failure or wear can prevent correct operation.
Incorrect sensor readings or control programs can cause an inappropriate action.
Requires suitable power, installation and maintenance.
